name: King Oyster: thick-stem method
summary: Paid example recipe: cooler, drier fruiting to favor thick stems.
notes: Demo premium profile for the community store. Same species as the free king oyster card.
chamber_notes: Top-fruit in a shallow tray or restrict side pins. Top-dress with a thin casing if stems stay skinny.

source_notes.title: Stamets
source_notes.detail: Paul Stamets, Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms (commonly cited chamber ranges). Stem morphology in P. eryngii responds to CO2 and humidity.

source_notes.title: Practice
source_notes.detail: Growers often drop humidity into the low 80s after pins set and keep fresh air moderate, not oyster-high.

stages.name: Pinning
stages.notes: Fewer, larger pins beat a full flush of thin fruits.

light_recipe.why: Same dark spawn run as other oysters. Fruiting is blue-heavy because P. eryngii primordia respond to blue light. Hours and white percent are the oyster default (12 h, 20% / 92 lux). No king-oyster-specific lux was found.
light_recipe.wavelength_note: WS2812 blue is roughly 465 to 475 nm. The RGB mix is an approximation of cited wavelengths, not a measured spectrum.

sources.title: Xie 2018 king oyster
sources.detail: Chunliang Xie et al., Comparative transcriptomics of Pleurotus eryngii reveals blue-light regulation of CAZymes at primordium differentiated into fruiting body stage, Gene 646 (2018). Blue light induced primordium differentiation.

sources.title: Penn State oyster production
sources.detail: Daniel J. Royse, Cultivation of Oyster Mushrooms, Penn State College of Agricultural Sciences. First 12 to 21 days of spawn run may be completed without artificial lighting. After spawn run, 4 h of cool white fluorescent light at 50 to 300 lux may be provided. This recipe uses 12 h for fruiting (Stamets) and maps 20% white to 92 lux, inside that 50 to 300 lux band.

sources.title: Stamets
sources.detail: Paul Stamets, Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms, Ten Speed Press. Spawn run is described as dark. Fruiting is commonly cited as about 12 h light.

sources.title: Sakamoto 2018
sources.detail: Yuichi Sakamoto, Influences of environmental factors on fruiting body induction, development and maturation in mushroom-forming fungi, Fungal Biology Reviews 32 (2018). Light is a fruiting cue for many basidiomycetes. Blue light is the usual photomorphogenesis signal. Agaricus bisporus is called out as not needing light for a cap. Flammulina velutipes can fruit in the dark as a long stem with a tiny cap.
